sources.title: Jamestown-Yorktown Foundation: Paspahegh Town
sources.note: Museum reconstruction based on excavated Paspahegh, Native oral tradition and seventeenth-century English descriptions. More than 30 groups in paramount chiefdom; not evidence that it already existed in 1492.

sources.title: National Park Service: chronology of Powhatan activity
sources.note: Pre-1607 and 1607 entries on inherited six tribes, expansion through alliances/coercion, distinct constituent groups. Later war and treaty chronology. Population estimates not adopted.

sources.title: National Park Service: Life in the Indigenous Chesapeake
sources.note: Regional context: matrilineal leadership, women chiefs, seasonal work and food resources. Draft avoids assigning every Chesapeake custom to every Powhatan person.

sources.title: William & Mary: Werowocomoco 2003 excavations
sources.note: Original excavation report: shell-tempered fabric-impressed and stamped pottery; house-post traces, hearths and pits; sapling frames and mats. Werowocomoco is distinguished from Powhatan village near Richmond.

sources.title: Jamestown-Yorktown Foundation: Jamestown Settlement self-guide
sources.note: Printed page 6, Paspahegh Town: outdoor cooking, canoe uses, vessels up to 40 feet long, burning and shell scraping. Indexed original PDF text.

sources.title: Pamunkey artist Ethan Brown: Gourd Art
sources.note: First-person tribal artist account hosted by NPS, 2022. Child crop-watch platform, 1932 pottery school and ongoing community. Artistic interpretation explicitly identified rather than treated as an eyewitness picture of 1600.

sources.title: National Park Service: Pocahontas, her life and legend
sources.note: Daily skills and mussel-shell shaving; 1608 to 1609 drought reduced harvests and increased conflict over food. Avoid disputed rescue narrative and romantic reconstruction.

sources.title: Oklahoma State University: Powhatan Treaty, 1646
sources.note: Primary text, October 5, 1646: Necotowance, Crown subordination, governor confirmation of successors and annual twenty beaver skins. Political subordination not disappearance.

sources.title: National Park Service: Captain John Smith Chesapeake Trail brochure
sources.note: Direct fetch failed; indexed original exact query site:nps.gov "suckahanna" supplies panel A Small, Open Boat: Smith and Strachey recorded suckahanna for water. Colonial Latin-letter transcription, not Indigenous manuscript or reconstructed sentence.

sources.title: Nation Wendat: history and culture
sources.note: Direct community account, especially Maison longue and continuing community. No current population figures or broad claimed influence on US constitutional design copied.

sources.title: Ronald F. Williamson: The Archaeological History of the Wendat, Ontario Archaeology 94 (2014)
sources.note: Direct scholarly PDF: printed page 11/PDF index 9 sweat lodges; printed page 21/index19 Mantle ceramics and possible diverse residents; printed page42/index40 dispersal and descendants. Exact older Mantle dating avoided because subsequent chronological work revised it.

sources.title: Canadian Museum of History: Iroquoian food production
sources.note: Original museum page: Huron-Wendat maize reliance and agricultural surplus for bad harvests/trade. Exact percentage not used.

sources.title: Huronia Historical Parks: historic background and Wendat life
sources.note: Direct food/fishing/family-life sections, and 1649 mission abandonment. Does not adopt erroneous opening phrase calling Wendat a branch of Haudenosaunee, fixed dimensions, broad universal marriage claims or totalizing accounts of childhood discipline.

sources.title: Sainte-Marie among the Hurons: mission history
sources.note: Official Ontario historic-site account: 1639 establishment, French Jesuit headquarters, palisaded workshops/church/residences and 1649 burning/abandonment. Not treated as a typical Wendat town.

sources.title: Wyandotte Nation: Our History
sources.note: Community-authored distinction between historical Wendat confederacy and later Wyandotte identity formed from Tionontati, Attignawantan and Wenro survivors in 1649 to 1650. No blanket alias grouping or adoption of source’s mistaken number for original Haudenosaunee nations.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Huron tray, circa 1860
sources.note: Direct catalogue 2011.154.96, Quebec, circa1860, birchbark and moosehair. No invented maker name or exact-year event.

sources.title: Nation Wendat: community archives
sources.note: Direct Fonds François Vincent description: dictionaries, phonetic transcriptions, petitions, maps, correspondence and treaty materials.

sources.title: Nation Wendat: École Wahta’
sources.note: Direct modern community school page, cultural activities and language from kindergarten. Avoid current fees, officeholders and exact teaching frequency.

sources.title: Nation Wendat: language and revitalization
sources.note: Direct dictionary list gives Kwatatiah! « Parlons! ». English Let’s speak! translated from that supplied French gloss. Explicit contemporary community orthography, not an ancient inscription; page describes nineteenth-century dormancy and modern revitalization.

batchIdentityNotes.assessment: Missing and collision-checked. Indexed 1492 to 1500 polygon bbox -77.6510 to -77.2118, 37.4161 to 37.6346 is a very small Richmond-area outline, consistent with local Powhatan associations rather than the full Tidewater paramount chiefdom. Public opening distinguishes local people/town, ruler and later network and does not claim later confederacy existed at 1492. Wider dated history provides the useful narrative; Werowocomoco is only a named archaeological example, not an absorbed alias. No modern constituent nation is erased by a conquest ending.

Missing and collision-checked. Indexed 1500 to 1530, decoded world1500 outline bbox -85.5063 to -70.7137, 41.9451 to 50.2322 greatly exceeds a plausible contemporary Wendat confederacy border; public caveat says so. Huron is a historical outsider label; display uses Wendat (Huron). Modern Wendake community and later Wyandotte Nation have connected but nonidentical histories. No aliases absorbed: Wendake-Nionwentsio, Wyandot-Anderdon and Wyandotte-Oklahoma remain separate records. Primary Wyandotte self-history specifically cautions against equating its formation with the historical Huron Confederacy. Modern language sample explicitly marked contemporary.
